court: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber

facts.text: The applicant, Mr İzzet Çakıcı, is a Turkish citizen born in 1953, living in Diyarbakır, south-east Turkey, who lodged an application on his own behalf and on behalf of his brother Ahmet Çakıcı, who allegedly disappeared under circumstances engaging State responsibility.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  The applicant, Mr İzzet Çakıcı, is a Turkish citizen who was born in 1953 and is at present living in Diyarbakır in south-east Turkey. His application to the Commission was brought on his own behalf and on behalf of his brother Ahmet Çakıcı, who, he alleges, has disappeared in circumstances engaging the responsibility of the State.

facts.text: On 8 November 1993, Ahmet Çakıcı was detained during a security operation in the village of Çitlibahçe by gendarmes and village guards; he hid initially but was caught leaving a house and taken from the village by security forces.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  On 8 November 1993, the applicant’s brother, Ahmet Çakıcı, was detained during an operation in the village of Çitlibahçe carried out by gendarmes and village guards. When the operation commenced early in the morning, Ahmet Çakıcı hid in a house near the fountain while the other men were gathered in an open area. The security forces began setting fire to the houses. Ahmet Çakıcı retrieved money, 4,700,000 Turkish liras (TRL), which he had hidden in the roof of his house and was caught leaving the house. Ahmet Çakıcı was taken from the village by the security forces. This was witnessed by the other villagers.

facts.text: Ahmet Çakıcı was taken first to Hazro, kept overnight, then to Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie headquarters where he was detained for about 85 days, during which he was beaten and tortured, including electric shocks.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  Ahmet Çakıcı was first taken to Hazro, where he was kept overnight before being taken to Diyarbakır. In Diyarbakır, he was detained at the provincial gendarmerie headquarters. After about six to seven days, he was held for sixteen to seventeen days in the same room as Mustafa Engin, Abdurrahman Al and Tahsin Demirbaş, who had been taken into custody on 8 November 1993 by the security forces in an operation at Bağlan. Ahmet Çakıcı had been beaten, a rib being broken and his head split open. He was taken out of the room for interrogation on several occasions, when he received electric shocks and was beaten.

facts.text: After about 85 days at Diyarbakır, Ahmet Çakıcı was taken back to Hazro, detained for several months, then moved to Kavaklıboğaz gendarmerie station where he was seen during a 13-day period in spring or early summer 1994 by another detainee.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  After eighty-five days at the provincial gendarmerie headquarters, in or about late January-early February 1994, Ahmet Çakıcı was taken back to Hazro where he was detained for several months. From there he was moved to the gendarmerie station at Kavaklıboğaz. During a period of thirteen days in or about spring or early summer 1994, Hikmet Aksoy, who was also detained at Kavaklıboğaz, saw Ahmet Çakıcı when they were taken out of the cells for meals.

facts.text: In May 1996, the applicant learned that authorities claimed Ahmet Çakıcı had been killed in a clash between 17 and 19 February 1995 on Kıllıboğan Hill, based solely on finding his identification card on a body.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  In May 1996, following the transmission of Government submissions, the applicant learned for the first time that it was claimed by the authorities that Ahmet Çakıcı had been killed in a clash between 17 and 19 February 1995 on Kıllıboğan Hill, Hani. The identification appeared to be based solely on the claim that Ahmet Çakıcı’s identification card was found on one of the bodies.

facts.text: The Government stated Ahmet Çakıcı was not taken into custody during the 8 November 1993 operation and was not detained at Hazro, Diyarbakır, or Kavaklıboğaz; custody records showed no detention.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  They state that Ahmet Çakıcı was not taken into custody by the security forces during the operation carried out at Çitlibahçe on 8 November 1993 and was not held in detention over any subsequent period. The custody records indicated that he was not held at Hazro or at Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie headquarters. Nor was he was taken to the gendarmerie station at Kavaklıboğaz.

facts.text: The Government claimed Ahmet Çakıcı was a militant PKK member found dead with 55 other militants at Kıllıboğan Hill after a clash between 17 and 19 February 1995, implicated in killing five teachers on 23 October 1993.

anchor.surface_text: 20.  Ahmet Çakıcı was a militant member of the PKK organisation. Following an armed clash between the PKK and the security forces on 17 to 19 February 1995, he had been found dead with fifty-five other militants at Kıllıboğan Hill. Ahmet Çakıcı had been implicated in the killing on 23 October 1993 of five teachers from Dadaş whom he had reportedly described as “servile dogs of the State”.

facts.text: No complaint was made to the public prosecutor at Hazro by any member of the applicant’s family regarding the alleged disappearance.

anchor.surface_text: 21.   No complaint was made to the public prosecutor at Hasro by any member of the applicant’s family in respect of the alleged disappearance.

facts.text: On 22 December 1993, Tevfik Çakıcı, father of the applicant and Ahmet, submitted a handwritten petition to Diyarbakır National Security Court requesting information about Ahmet’s fate; he was orally told Ahmet was not in custody lists.

anchor.surface_text: 25.   On 22 December 1993, Tevfik Çakıcı, the father of the applicant and Ahmet Çakıcı, submitted a handwritten petition to the Diyarbakır National Security Court requesting information as to what had happened to Ahmet Çakıcı, who had been taken into custody on 8 November 1993 by the security forces at the same time as Mustafa Engin, Abdurrahman Al and Tahsin Demirbaş, who had been released twenty-four days later. An oral reply was given to him that Ahmet Çakıcı was not on the list of persons in custody.

facts.text: By letters dated 4 and 19 April 1994, Hazro public prosecutor informed Diyarbakır National Security Court that Ahmet Çakıcı had not been taken into custody or detained on 8 November 1993 and no application had been filed by his family regarding his disappearance.

anchor.surface_text:
26.  By letter dated 4 April 1994, the Hazro public prosecutor, Aydın Tekin, informed the Chief Public Prosecutor at the Diyarbakır National Security Court that, on examination of their records, Ahmet Çakıcı had not been taken into custody or detained on 8 November 1993.

27.  By letter dated 19 April 1994 to the Chief Public Prosecutor at the Diyarbakır National Security Court, the Hazro public prosecutor, Aydın Tekin, confirmed his letter of 4 April 1994 and stated that no application had been filed by Ahmet Çakıcı’s family to the effect that he was missing.

facts.text: On 9 September 1994, the applicant gave a statement to a public prosecutor stating his brother had been taken into custody on 8 November 1993 and seen by other detainees; on 25 November 1994, Remziye Çakıcı also stated gendarmes had taken her husband during the operation.

anchor.surface_text: 29.  On 9 September 1994, the applicant’s statement was taken by a public prosecutor at Diyarbakır. In his statement, he stated that his brother Ahmet Çakıcı had been taken into custody by soldiers on 8 November 1993 and that he had been seen by Mustafa Engin and Tahsin Demirbaş, who were also detained. On 25 November 1994, the public prosecutor took a statement from Remziye Çakıcı. She stated that gendarmes had taken away her husband during an operation on 8 November 1993.

facts.text: By letter dated 1 December 1994, Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie command informed the Attorney-General that records indicated Ahmet Çakıcı had not been detained on 8 November 1993.

anchor.surface_text: 30.  By letter dated 1 December 1994, Colonel Eşref Hatipoğlu of Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie command informed the Diyarbakır Attorney-General, in reply to a letter of enquiry of 22 November 1994, that their records indicated that Ahmet Çakıcı had not been detained on 8 November 1994 [error for 1993].

facts.text: By letter dated 23 June 1995, Hazro district gendarmerie command stated Ahmet Çakıcı was a PKK member found dead during operations at Kıllıboğan Hill on 17-19 February 1995, identified by identity card found on a body.

anchor.surface_text: 37.  By letter dated 23 June 1995 to the Hazro public prosecutor, the district gendarmerie command at Hazro referred to the prosecutor’s enquiry dated 22 May 1995 about the whereabouts of Ahmet Çakıcı and to the letter dated 1 March 1995 from the Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie command. It stated that Ahmet Çakıcı had been a member of the PKK. Following an operation carried out at Kıllıboğan Hill on 17-19 February which resulted in the deaths of fifty-six terrorists, Ahmet Çakıcı’s identity was established by the identity card located amongst the documents found on the body of a terrorist. It was concluded that he was one of the terrorists.

facts.text: By decision of 13 June 1996, Hazro public prosecutor issued a decision of lack of jurisdiction and transferred the file to the District Administrative Council; the investigation noted Ahmet Çakıcı was a PKK member found dead at Kıllıboğan Hill and suspects were unidentified individuals of Hazro gendarmerie and village guards.

anchor.surface_text: 42.  By decision of 13 June 1996, Hazro public prosecutor Mustafa Turhan issued a decision of lack of jurisdiction and transferred the file to the District Administrative Council. The decision named the applicant and Remziye Çakıcı as the complainants and identified the victim as Ahmet Çakıcı. The offence was described as ill-treatment, torture and confiscation of money of a detainee and the defendants as unidentified individuals of Hazro gendarmerie station and village guards. It stated that the complainants claimed that soldiers from Hazro gendarmerie command arrived in Çitlibahçe on the morning of 8 November 1993 and detained the victim, that the victim had been taken to Diyarbakır where he was tortured and that a lieutenant had removed TRL 4,280,000 from him. The investigation had established that the victim was a member of the PKK terrorist organisation and that following an operation by the security forces in the Kıllıboğan Hill region on 17 and 19 February the victim’s identity card had been located on one of the dead terrorists, thus confirming the individual’s identity as Ahmet Çakıcı without doubt.

facts.text: The Commission conducted its own investigation, examined documents, and took oral evidence from eleven witnesses including the applicant, villagers, detainees, gendarmerie officers, and public prosecutors.

anchor.surface_text: 43.  Since the facts of the case were disputed, particularly concerning the events in or around November 1993, the Commission conducted an investigation, with the assistance of the parties, and accepted documentary evidence, including written statements and oral evidence taken from eleven witnesses: the applicant; Fevzi Okatan, previous muhtar of Çitlibahçe; Remziye Çakıcı, the wife of Ahmet Çakıcı; Mustafa Engin, who had been detained at Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie headquarters from 9 November to 1 December 1993; Ertan Altınoluk, who had been gendarmerie commander of Hazro in November 1993 and had commanded the operation at Çitlibahçe on 8 November 1993; Mehmet Bitgin, a villager from Çitlibahçe; Mustafa Turhan, public prosecutor in Hazro from November 1994;  Aytekin Türker, the Hazro central station commander at Hazro district gendarmerie headquarters from July 1993 to August 1994; Ahmet Katmerkaya, the gendarme responsible for keeping the custody records at Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie headquarters since August 1992; Kemal Çavdar, a gendarme who had served at Kavaklıboğaz station from July 1993 to August 1995; and Abdullah Cebeci, the brother of the imam who had been kidnapped with five teachers from Dadaş.

facts.text: The Commission found that Ahmet Çakıcı was taken into custody by Hazro gendarmes on 8 November 1993, based on credible witness testimony from villagers and detainees.

anchor.surface_text: 47.  The Commission assessed the evidence of the witnesses from the village, Remziye Çakıcı, Fevzi Okatan and Mehmet Bitgin, who stated that they saw Ahmet Çakıcı being taken from the village by the gendarmes, as being on the whole consistent, credible and convincing. They found the Government’s objections to their credibility to be unfounded on examination. Accordingly, the Commission found that when the gendarmes arrived in Çitlibahçe on 8 November 1993, Ahmet Çakıcı attempted to hide but was found and taken from the village in custody by the Hazro gendarmes.

facts.text: The Commission accepted the oral evidence of Mustafa Engin that he saw and spoke to Ahmet Çakıcı detained in Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie headquarters for 16-17 days, who was in bad condition and had been beaten and tortured.

anchor.surface_text: 50.  The Commission accepted the oral evidence of Mustafa Engin, who stated that while he was detained at Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie headquarters he saw and spoke to Ahmet Çakıcı, who was detained over a period of sixteen to seventeen days in the same room. It also accepted his evidence that Ahmet Çakıcı looked in a bad condition, with dried blood on his clothes, and that Ahmet Çakıcı had told him that he had been beaten, one of his ribs broken, his head split open and that he had been given electric shocks twice.

Article 2 of the Convention, which safeguards the right to life, ranks as one of the most fundamental provisions in the Convention and, together with Article 3 of the Convention, enshrines one of the basic values of the democratic societies making up the Council of Europe... The obligation imposed is not exclusively concerned with intentional killing resulting from the use of force by agents of the State but also extends, in the first sentence of Article 2 § 1, to imposing a positive obligation on States that the right to life be protected by law.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that his brother had been taken into unacknowledged detention and had since disappeared in circumstances which disclosed a violation of Article 2 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: Article 2 of the Convention, which safeguards the right to life, ranks as one of the most fundamental provisions in the Convention

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the Commission's findings that Ahmet Çakıcı was the victim of unacknowledged detention and serious ill-treatment, concluding beyond reasonable doubt that he died following apprehension and detention by security forces, thus violating Article 2.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that in respect of detained persons a government assumed a special obligation for their safety and their right to life and that there was a positive obligation on them to account for the detainee and produce him alive.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant referred to the Commission’s findings that his brother Ahmet Çakıcı had been ill-treated during an unacknowledged detention and that the authorities had claimed that he was dead as disclosing a very strong probability that his brother had died in circumstances for which the authorities were responsible.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court reiterated that Article 2 imposes a positive obligation on States to protect the right to life, including effective official investigation when individuals have been killed as a result of the use of force.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that the failure to provide an effective investigation into the circumstances of Ahmet Çakıcı’s detention disclosed an additional breach of Article 2.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant referred to the Commission’s findings that his brother Ahmet Çakıcı had been ill-treated during an unacknowledged detention and that the authorities had claimed that he was dead as disclosing a very strong probability that his brother had died in circumstances for which the authorities were responsible.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found a violation of Article 2 also due to the lack of effective procedural safeguards disclosed by the inadequate investigation carried out into the disappearance and alleged finding of Ahmet Çakıcı’s body.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that Article 2 could not be properly invoked in the present case, relying on the Court’s approach in the Kurt case where there was a lack of concrete indications that the applicant’s son had met his death during unacknowledged detention.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that Article 2 could not be properly invoked in the present case, relying, inter alia, on the Court’s approach in the Kurt case (Kurt judgment cited above, p. 1182, § 107), where there was found to be a lack of concrete indications that the applicant’s son had met his death during his unacknowledged detention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court distinguished the present case from Kurt, finding sufficient circumstantial evidence beyond reasonable doubt that Ahmet Çakıcı died following detention by security forces.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the McCann case demonstrated the applicability of Article 2 only where security forces were established as having caused the death, which was not the position here.

anchor.surface_text: The Government also referred to the McCann case (McCann and Others v. the United Kingdom judgment of 27 September 1995, Series A no. 324) as demonstrating the applicability of Article 2 in circumstances where the security forces were established as having caused the death of the person concerned, which, they argued, was not the position in this case.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found sufficient circumstantial evidence to conclude State responsibility for death, thus rejecting the Government's argument.

arguments.claim: The applicant alleged that his brother had been subjected to serious ill-treatment amounting to torture while detained, including beatings and electric shocks, and that failure to investigate constituted a breach of Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: Article 3 of the Convention, which provides: “No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.”

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found beyond reasonable doubt that Ahmet Çakıcı was tortured during his detention, constituting a violation of Article 3.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted criticisms of the Commission’s assessment of facts and alleged failure to apply a strict standard of interpretation regarding Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: The Government’s submissions on this aspect were restricted to their criticisms of the Commission’s assessment of the facts and of its alleged failure to apply a strict standard of interpretation in keeping with the case-law regarding Article 3 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the Commission's assessment and found the witness evidence credible and reliable.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that the disappearance of his brother constituted inhuman treatment in relation to himself and other family members due to lack of information and prolonged uncertainty.

anchor.surface_text: Relying, inter alia, on the Court’s judgment in the Kurt case (Kurt judgment cited above, pp. 1187-88, §§ 130-34), the applicant complained that the disappearance of his brother constituted inhuman treatment in relation to himself and other members of the family, including Remziye, Ahmet Çakıcı’s wife, and their children.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no special features justifying an additional violation of Article 3 in relation to the applicant himself.

arguments.claim: The Government disputed that the applicant might claim to be an indirect victim of a violation of the rights of his brother and argued the links were not particularly close.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court examined the complaint but found no violation as concerns the applicant himself.
